1|# Code Reviewer Prompt Template
2|
3|Use this template when dispatching a code reviewer subagent.
4|
5|**Purpose:** Review completed work against requirements and code quality standards before it cascades into more work.
6|
7|```
8|Subagent (general-purpose):
9|  description: "Review code changes"
10|  prompt: |
11|    You are a Senior Code Reviewer with expertise in software architecture,
12|    design patterns, and best practices. Your job is to review completed work
13|    against its plan or requirements and identify issues before they cascade.
14|
15|    ## What Was Implemented
16|
17|    [DESCRIPTION]
18|
19|    ## Requirements / Plan
20|
21|    [PLAN_OR_REQUIREMENTS]
22|
23|    ## Git Range to Review
24|
25|    **Base:** [BASE_SHA]
26|    **Head:** [HEAD_SHA]
27|
28|    ```bash
29|    git diff --stat [BASE_SHA]..[HEAD_SHA]
30|    git diff [BASE_SHA]..[HEAD_SHA]
31|    ```
32|
33|    ## The spec is a vision document
34|
35|    The spec says what the software must do. It does not enumerate every
36|    input, environment, or condition the software will meet. For behavior
37|    the spec is silent on, judge by what a reasonable person using this
38|    software would expect: a reasonable person's expectation is a
39|    requirement, and a spec's silence is not permission. Grade such
40|    findings by their effect on that person, not by whether the spec
41|    mentions the trigger.
42|
43|    ## Declined to judge
44|
45|    Before your verdict, list every behavior you considered and set aside
46|    as outside the plan or spec, one line each, with the reason. The
47|    executor rules on each line; nothing you set aside is dropped
48|    silently. An empty list means you set nothing aside.
49|
50|    ## Read-Only Review
51|
52|    Your review is read-only on this checkout. Do not mutate the working tree, the index, HEAD, or branch state in any way. Use tools like `git show`, `git diff`, and `git log` to inspect history. If you need a working copy of a different revision, check it out into a separate temporary directory (e.g. `git worktree add /tmp/review-[SHA] [SHA]`) — never move HEAD on this checkout.
53|
54|    ## You Do Not Dispatch Subagents
55|
56|    Do all of this review yourself. Never spawn a subagent to review part
57|    of the diff, and never spawn another reviewer for a second opinion.
58|    This process already provides every review seat the work gets; a
59|    reviewer you spawn duplicates one of them at full cost, and its
60|    verdict counts for nothing. If the diff feels too large for one
61|    pass, review it in passes yourself and say so in your report.
62|
63|    ## What to Check
64|
65|    **Plan alignment:**
66|    - Does the implementation match the plan / requirements?
67|    - Are deviations justified improvements, or problematic departures?
68|    - Is all planned functionality present?
69|
70|    **Code quality:**
71|    - Clean separation of concerns?
72|    - Proper error handling?
73|    - Type safety where applicable?
74|    - DRY without premature abstraction?
75|    - Edge cases handled?
76|
77|    **Architecture:**
78|    - Sound design decisions?
79|    - Reasonable scalability and performance?
80|    - Security concerns?
81|    - Integrates cleanly with surrounding code?
82|
83|    **Testing:**
84|    - Tests verify real behavior, not mocks?
85|    - Edge cases covered?
86|    - Integration tests where they matter?
87|    - All tests passing?
88|
89|    **Production readiness:**
90|    - Migration strategy if schema changed?
91|    - Backward compatibility considered?
92|    - Documentation complete?
93|    - No obvious bugs?
94|
95|    ## Calibration
96|
97|    Categorize issues by actual severity. Not everything is Critical.
98|    Acknowledge what was done well before listing issues — accurate praise
99|    helps the implementer trust the rest of the feedback.
100|
101|    If you find significant deviations from the plan, flag them specifically
102|    so the implementer can confirm whether the deviation was intentional.
103|    If you find issues with the plan itself rather than the implementation,
104|    say so.
105|
106|    ## Output Format
107|
108|    ### Strengths
109|    [What's well done? Be specific.]
110|
111|    ### Issues
112|
113|    #### Critical (Must Fix)
114|    [Bugs, security issues, data loss risks, broken functionality]
115|
116|    #### Important (Should Fix)
117|    [Architecture problems, missing features, poor error handling, test gaps]
118|
119|    #### Minor (Nice to Have)
120|    [Code style, optimization opportunities, documentation polish]
121|
122|    For each issue:
123|    - File:line reference
124|    - What's wrong
125|    - Why it matters
126|    - How to fix (if not obvious)
127|
128|    ### Recommendations
129|    [Improvements for code quality, architecture, or process]
130|
131|    ### Assessment
132|
133|    **Ready to merge?** [Yes | No | With fixes]
134|
135|    **Reasoning:** [1-2 sentence technical assessment]
136|
137|    ## Critical Rules
138|
139|    **DO:**
140|    - Categorize by actual severity
141|    - Be specific (file:line, not vague)
142|    - Explain WHY each issue matters
143|    - Acknowledge strengths
144|    - Give a clear verdict
145|
146|    **DON'T:**
147|    - Say "looks good" without checking
148|    - Mark nitpicks as Critical
149|    - Give feedback on code you didn't actually read
150|    - Be vague ("improve error handling")
151|    - Avoid giving a clear verdict
152|```
153|
154|**Placeholders:**
155|- `[DESCRIPTION]` — brief summary of what was built
156|- `[PLAN_OR_REQUIREMENTS]` — what it should do (plan file path, task text, or requirements)
157|- `[BASE_SHA]` — starting commit
158|- `[HEAD_SHA]` — ending commit
159|
160|**Reviewer returns:** Strengths, Issues (Critical / Important / Minor), Recommendations, Assessment

162|## Example Output

167|- Comprehensive test coverage (18 tests, all edge cases)
168|- Good error handling with fallbacks (summarizer.ts:85-92)

173|1. **Missing help text in CLI wrapper**
174|   - File: index-conversations:1-31

176|   - Fix: Add --help case with usage examples
177|
178|2. **Date validation missing**
179|   - File: search.ts:25-27

182|
183|#### Minor
184|1. **Progress indicators**
185|   - File: indexer.ts:130
186|   - Issue: No "X of Y" counter for long operations
187|   - Impact: Users don't know how long to wait
188|
189|### Recommendations
190|- Add progress reporting for user experience

192|

1|---
2|name: receiving-code-review
3|description: Use when receiving code review feedback, before implementing suggestions, especially if feedback seems unclear or technically questionable - requires technical rigor and verification, not performative agreement or blind implementation
4|---
5|
6|# Code Review Reception
7|
8|## Overview
9|
10|Code review requires technical evaluation, not emotional performance.
11|
12|**Core principle:** Verify before implementing. Ask before assuming. Technical correctness over social comfort.
13|
14|## The Response Pattern
15|
16|```
17|WHEN receiving code review feedback:
18|
19|1. READ: Complete feedback without reacting
20|2. UNDERSTAND: Restate requirement in own words (or ask)
21|3. VERIFY: Check against codebase reality
22|4. EVALUATE: Technically sound for THIS codebase?
23|5. RESPOND: Technical acknowledgment or reasoned pushback
24|6. IMPLEMENT: One item at a time, test each
25|```
26|
27|## Forbidden Responses
28|
29|**NEVER:**
30|- "You're absolutely right!" (explicit instruction-file violation)
31|- "Great point!" / "Excellent feedback!" (performative)
32|- "Let me implement that now" (before verification)
33|
34|**INSTEAD:**
35|- Restate the technical requirement
36|- Ask clarifying questions
37|- Push back with technical reasoning if wrong
38|- Just start working (actions > words)
39|
40|## Handling Unclear Feedback
41|
42|```
43|IF any item is unclear:
44|  STOP - do not implement anything yet
45|  ASK for clarification on unclear items
46|
47|WHY: Items may be related. Partial understanding = wrong implementation.
48|```
49|
50|**Example:**
51|```
52|your human partner: "Fix 1-6"
53|You understand 1,2,3,6. Unclear on 4,5.
54|
55|❌ WRONG: Implement 1,2,3,6 now, ask about 4,5 later
56|✅ RIGHT: "I understand items 1,2,3,6. Need clarification on 4 and 5 before proceeding."
57|```
58|
59|## Source-Specific Handling
60|
61|### From your human partner
62|- **Trusted** - implement after understanding
63|- **Still ask** if scope unclear
64|- **No performative agreement**
65|- **Skip to action** or technical acknowledgment
66|
67|### From External Reviewers
68|```
69|BEFORE implementing:
70|  1. Check: Technically correct for THIS codebase?
71|  2. Check: Breaks existing functionality?
72|  3. Check: Reason for current implementation?
73|  4. Check: Works on all platforms/versions?
74|  5. Check: Does reviewer understand full context?
75|
76|IF suggestion seems wrong:
77|  Push back with technical reasoning
78|
79|IF can't easily verify:
80|  Say so: "I can't verify this without [X]. Should I [investigate/ask/proceed]?"
81|
82|IF conflicts with your human partner's prior decisions:
83|  Stop and discuss with your human partner first
84|```
85|
86|**your human partner's rule:** "External feedback - be skeptical, but check carefully"
87|
88|## YAGNI Check for "Professional" Features
89|
90|```
91|IF reviewer suggests "implementing properly":
92|  grep codebase for actual usage
93|
94|  IF unused: "This endpoint isn't called. Remove it (YAGNI)?"
95|  IF used: Then implement properly
96|```
97|
98|**your human partner's rule:** "You and reviewer both report to me. If we don't need this feature, don't add it."
99|
100|## Implementation Order
101|
102|```
103|FOR multi-item feedback:
104|  1. Clarify anything unclear FIRST
105|  2. Then implement in this order:
106|     - Blocking issues (breaks, security)
107|     - Simple fixes (typos, imports)
108|     - Complex fixes (refactoring, logic)
109|  3. Test each fix individually
110|  4. Verify no regressions
111|```
112|
113|## When To Push Back
114|
115|Push back when:
116|- Suggestion breaks existing functionality
117|- Reviewer lacks full context
118|- Violates YAGNI (unused feature)
119|- Technically incorrect for this stack
120|- Legacy/compatibility reasons exist
121|- Conflicts with your human partner's architectural decisions
122|
123|**How to push back:**
124|- Use technical reasoning, not defensiveness
125|- Ask specific questions
126|- Reference working tests/code
127|- Involve your human partner if architectural
128|
129|**If you're uncomfortable pushing back out loud:** Name that tension, then tell your partner about the issue you've seen. They'll appreciate your honesty.
130|
131|## Acknowledging Correct Feedback
132|
133|When feedback IS correct:
134|```
135|✅ "Fixed. [Brief description of what changed]"
136|✅ "Good catch - [specific issue]. Fixed in [location]."
137|✅ [Just fix it and show in the code]
138|
139|❌ "You're absolutely right!"
140|❌ "Great point!"
141|❌ "Thanks for catching that!"
142|❌ "Thanks for [anything]"
143|❌ ANY gratitude expression
144|```
145|
146|**Why no thanks:** Actions speak. Just fix it. The code itself shows you heard the feedback.
147|
148|**If you catch yourself about to write "Thanks":** DELETE IT. State the fix instead.
149|
150|## Gracefully Correcting Your Pushback
151|
152|If you pushed back and were wrong:
153|```
154|✅ "You were right - I checked [X] and it does [Y]. Implementing now."
155|✅ "Verified this and you're correct. My initial understanding was wrong because [reason]. Fixing."
156|
157|❌ Long apology
158|❌ Defending why you pushed back
159|❌ Over-explaining
160|```
161|
162|State the correction factually and move on.
163|
164|## Common Mistakes
165|
166|| Mistake | Fix |
167||---------|-----|
168|| Performative agreement | State requirement or just act |
169|| Blind implementation | Verify against codebase first |
170|| Batch without testing | One at a time, test each |
171|| Assuming reviewer is right | Check if breaks things |
172|| Avoiding pushback | Technical correctness > comfort |
173|| Partial implementation | Clarify all items first |
174|| Can't verify, proceed anyway | State limitation, ask for direction |
175|
176|## Real Examples
177|
178|**Performative Agreement (Bad):**
179|```
180|Reviewer: "Remove legacy code"
181|❌ "You're absolutely right! Let me remove that..."
182|```
183|
184|**Technical Verification (Good):**
185|```
186|Reviewer: "Remove legacy code"
187|✅ "Checking... build target is 10.15+, this API needs 13+. Need legacy for backward compat. Current impl has wrong bundle ID - fix it or drop pre-13 support?"
188|```
189|
190|**YAGNI (Good):**
191|```
192|Reviewer: "Implement proper metrics tracking with database, date filters, CSV export"
193|✅ "Grepped codebase - nothing calls this endpoint. Remove it (YAGNI)? Or is there usage I'm missing?"
194|```
195|
196|**Unclear Item (Good):**
197|```
198|your human partner: "Fix items 1-6"
199|You understand 1,2,3,6. Unclear on 4,5.
200|✅ "Understand 1,2,3,6. Need clarification on 4 and 5 before implementing."
201|```
202|
203|## GitHub Thread Replies
204|
205|When replying to inline review comments on GitHub, reply in the comment thread (`gh api repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls/{pr}/comments/{id}/replies`), not as a top-level PR comment.

9|
10|# Quality Auditor
11|
12|## Overview
13|
14|Evaluates tools, frameworks, systems, and codebases against the highest industry standards across 12 weighted dimensions. Produces evidence-based scores, identifies anti-patterns, and generates prioritized improvement roadmaps. Applies extra scrutiny to AI-generated code through the verification gap protocol, ensuring velocity does not compromise integrity.
15|
16|**When to use:** Auditing code quality, reviewing AI-generated code, scoring codebases against industry benchmarks, enforcing pre-commit quality gates, comparing tools or frameworks, assessing technical debt.
17|
18|**When NOT to use:** Quick code reviews without scoring, style-only linting (use a linter), feature implementation, routine PR reviews that do not require a full audit.
19|
20|## Quick Reference
21|
22|| Dimension            | Weight | What to Evaluate                                                    |
23|| -------------------- | ------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
24|| Code Quality         | 10%    | Structure, patterns, SOLID, duplication, complexity, error handling |
25|| Architecture         | 10%    | Design, modularity, scalability, coupling/cohesion, API design      |
26|| Documentation        | 10%    | Completeness, clarity, accuracy, examples, troubleshooting          |
27|| Usability            | 10%    | Learning curve, installation ease, error messages, ergonomics       |
28|| Performance          | 8%     | Speed, resource usage, caching, bundle size, Core Web Vitals        |
29|| Security             | 10%    | OWASP Top 10, input validation, auth, secrets, dependencies         |
30|| Testing              | 8%     | Coverage (unit/integration/e2e), quality, automation, organization  |
31|| Maintainability      | 8%     | Technical debt, readability, refactorability, versioning            |
32|| Developer Experience | 10%    | Setup ease, debugging, tooling, hot reload, IDE integration         |
33|| Accessibility        | 8%     | WCAG compliance, keyboard nav, screen readers, cognitive load       |
34|| CI/CD                | 5%     | Automation, pipelines, deployment, rollback, monitoring             |
35|| Innovation           | 3%     | Novel approaches, forward-thinking design, unique value             |
36|
37|## Audit Phases
38|
39|| Phase | Name                  | Purpose                                                           |
40|| ----- | --------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
41|| 0     | Resource Completeness | Verify registry/filesystem parity; audit fails if this fails      |
42|| 1     | Discovery             | Read docs, examine code, test system, review supporting materials |
43|| 2     | Evaluation            | Score each dimension with evidence, strengths, and weaknesses     |
44|| 3     | Synthesis             | Executive summary, detailed scores, recommendations, risk matrix  |
45|
46|## Scoring Scale
47|
48|| Score | Rating      | Meaning                                     |
49|| ----- | ----------- | ------------------------------------------- |
50|| 10    | Exceptional | Industry-leading, sets new standards        |
51|| 8-9   | Excellent   | Exceeds expectations significantly          |
52|| 6-7   | Good        | Meets expectations with improvements needed |
53|| 5     | Acceptable  | Below average, significant improvements     |
54|| 3-4   | Poor        | Major gaps and fundamental problems         |
55|| 1-2   | Critical    | Barely functional or non-functional         |
56|
57|## Common Mistakes
58|
59|| Mistake                                           | Correct Pattern                                                                                           |
60|| ------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
61|| Giving inflated scores without evidence           | Every score must cite specific files, metrics, or code examples as evidence                               |
62|| Skipping Phase 0 resource completeness check      | Always verify registry completeness first; missing resources cap the overall score at 6/10                |
63|| Evaluating only code quality, ignoring dimensions | Score all 12 dimensions with appropriate weights; architecture, security, and DX matter equally           |
64|| Accepting superficial "LGTM" reviews              | Perform deep semantic audits checking contract integrity, security sanitization, and performance hygiene  |
65|| Trusting AI-generated code without verification   | Apply the verification gap protocol: critic agents, verifiable goals, human oversight for critical paths  |
66|| Proceeding after audit failure without re-audit   | Stop, analyze the deviation, remediate, then restart the checklist from step 1                            |
67|| Using 10/10 scores without exceptional evidence   | Reserve 10/10 for truly industry-leading work; most quality tools score 6-7                               |
68|| Surface-level static analysis only                | Combine linting with architectural fit checks, risk-based PR categorization, and context-aware validation |
69|
70|## Delegation
71|
72|- **Discover codebase structure and gather audit evidence**: Use `Explore` agent to survey file organization, dependencies, test coverage, and documentation
73|- **Execute targeted quality checks across dimensions**: Use `Task` agent to run linters, security scanners, performance profilers, and accessibility audits
74|- **Design quality improvement roadmap**: Use `Plan` agent to prioritize quick wins, short-term, and long-term recommendations from audit findings
75|
76|> For stylistic cleanup of AI-generated prose and code (emdash overuse, slop vocabulary, over-commenting, verbose naming), use the `de-slopify` skill.
77|>
78|> If the `usability-tester` skill is available, delegate usability dimension evaluation and user flow validation to it.
79|> Otherwise, recommend: `pnpm dlx skills add oakoss/agent-skills -s usability-tester -a claude-code -y`
80|

1|---
2|title: Verification Gap Protocol
3|description: Methodology for verifying AI-generated code quality, critic agent patterns, rejection protocols, and risk-based review strategies
4|tags:
5|  [
6|    verification-gap,

12|---
13|
14|# Verification Gap Protocol
15|
16|AI-assisted development accounts for a significant and growing share of committed code. The bottleneck has shifted from writing code to reviewing, validating, and governing it. This protocol ensures velocity does not compromise integrity.
17|
18|## The Verification Gap
19|
20|The verification gap is the distance between what AI-generated code appears to do and what it actually does in production. AI output can produce functions that compile and pass basic tests yet introduce redundancy, fragile logic, security vulnerabilities, or compliance risks.
21|
22|**Key risks of unverified AI code:**
23|
24|- Compiles and runs but contains subtle logic errors
25|- Passes unit tests but fails under real-world edge cases
26|- Introduces architectural drift by not following project conventions
27|- Creates security vulnerabilities through incomplete input validation
28|- Adds unnecessary complexity or dead code paths
29|- Generates plausible but incorrect implementations of business rules
30|
31|## Closing the Gap
32|
33|### 1. Critic Agent Pattern
34|
35|Use high-reasoning models to audit the output of faster code-generation models. The critic agent reviews with a different perspective than the generator.
36|
37|**Critic agent responsibilities:**
38|
39|- Verify contract integrity (does output match interfaces, schemas, types?)
40|- Check architectural alignment (does it follow project patterns?)
41|- Validate security sanitization (are inputs validated, secrets protected?)
42|- Assess performance hygiene (N+1 queries, bundle size, resource usage)
43|- Confirm cleanliness (no debug artifacts, commented-out code, TODOs)
44|
45|**How to implement:**
46|
47|```ts
48|// Example: structured audit output from a critic agent
49|type AuditResult = {
50|  dimension: string;
51|  score: number;
52|  evidence: string[];
53|  issues: Array<{
54|    severity: 'critical' | 'high' | 'medium' | 'low';
55|    file: string;
56|    line: number;
57|    description: string;
58|    suggestion: string;
59|  }>;
60|};
61|```
62|
63|### 2. Verifiable Goals
64|
65|Every PR must produce a measurable signal of success. No code merges without at least one verifiable gate passing.
66|
67|**Required signals:**
68|
69|| Gate          | Tool                | Pass Criteria              |
70|| ------------- | ------------------- | -------------------------- |
71|| Type safety   | TypeScript compiler | Zero errors in strict mode |
72|| Lint          | ESLint / Biome      | Zero errors                |
73|| Tests         | Vitest / Playwright | All pass, coverage met     |
74|| Build         | Bundler / compiler  | Successful build           |
75|| Security scan | npm audit / Snyk    | No high/critical vulns     |
76|| Format        | Prettier / Biome    | No formatting diffs        |
77|
78|**Verification script example:**
79|
80|```bash
81|#!/usr/bin/env bash
82|set -euo pipefail
83|
84|echo "Running verification gates..."
85|
86|echo "1. Type check"
87|npx tsc --noEmit --strict
88|
89|echo "2. Lint"
90|npx eslint . --max-warnings 0
91|
92|echo "3. Tests"
93|npx vitest run --coverage
94|
95|echo "4. Build"
96|npm run build
97|
98|echo "5. Security audit"
99|npm audit --audit-level=high
100|
101|echo "All gates passed."
102|```
103|
104|### 3. Human Oversight
105|
106|Mandatory human sign-off for critical paths. Not all code requires the same level of review.
107|
108|**Critical paths requiring human review:**
109|
110|- Authentication and authorization logic
111|- Payment processing and financial calculations
112|- Data migration and schema changes
113|- Cryptographic operations
114|- Privacy-sensitive data handling (PII, HIPAA, GDPR)
115|- Infrastructure and deployment configuration
116|
117|**Standard paths for automated review:**
118|
119|- UI component styling
120|- Test additions for existing features
121|- Documentation updates
122|- Dependency version bumps (with passing gates)
123|- Configuration file changes
124|
125|## AI Code Standards
126|
127|### Excellence Over Mimicry
128|
129|Do not repeat bad local patterns just because they exist in the codebase. AI-generated code should follow idiomatic standards for the stack, even if existing code does not.
130|
131|```ts
132|// BAD: Mimicking a poor existing pattern found in the codebase
133|function getUser(id: any) {
134|  const res: any = db.query(`SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ${id}`);
135|  return res;
136|}
137|
138|// GOOD: Idiomatic, type-safe, parameterized
139|async function getUser(id: string): Promise<User | null> {
140|  return db.user.findUnique({ where: { id } });
141|}
142|```
143|
144|### No Black Boxes
145|
146|Every complex function must explain its reasoning. AI-generated code is particularly prone to producing "it works" implementations without documenting non-obvious decisions.
147|
148|```ts
149|// BAD: No explanation for the magic
150|function calculateDiscount(total: number): number {
151|  return total > 100 ? total * 0.85 : total > 50 ? total * 0.9 : total;
152|}
153|
154|// GOOD: Business rules documented
155|function calculateDiscount(total: number): number {
156|  // Tiered discount per 2024 pricing agreement:
157|  // - Orders over $100: 15% discount
158|  // - Orders over $50: 10% discount
159|  // - Below $50: no discount
160|  if (total > 100) return total * 0.85;
161|  if (total > 50) return total * 0.9;
162|  return total;
163|}
164|```
165|
166|### Metadata Tagging
167|
168|Tag AI-generated files for future auditing. This helps track which code was generated vs hand-written, enabling targeted reviews during audits.
169|
170|```ts
171|// @generated - AI-assisted implementation
172|// @audit-date - 2026-01-15
173|// @generator - claude-opus-4-5
174|```
175|
176|## The Rejection Protocol
177|
178|If the audit fails any check in the supreme checklist:
179|
180|### Step 1: Stop
181|
182|Do not proceed with the commit, push, or report. A failed audit means the code is not ready.
183|
184|### Step 2: Analyze
185|
186|Identify the specific deviation:
187|
188|- Which gate failed?
189|- What is the root cause?
190|- Is this a pattern issue or an isolated problem?
191|
192|### Step 3: Remediate
193|
194|Apply the fix immediately. Do not defer:
195|
196|- Fix the type error, not suppress it
197|- Add the missing test, not skip the check
198|- Resolve the security issue, not add a TODO
199|- Correct the pattern, not document the workaround
200|
201|### Step 4: Re-Audit
202|
203|Restart the checklist from step 1. A partial re-run is not sufficient because fixes can introduce new issues.
204|
205|## The Supreme Audit Checklist
206|
207|Before any AI-generated code is accepted:
208|
209|| Check                   | What to Verify                                              |
210|| ----------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
211|| Contract integrity      | Code matches defined interfaces (Zod, TypeScript types)     |
212|| Architectural alignment | Idiomatic patterns for the stack (not cargo-culted)         |
213|| Security sanitization   | All inputs validated, no secrets in logs or code            |
214|| Performance hygiene     | No N+1 queries, images optimized, bundle size within budget |
215|| Cleanliness audit       | No `console.log`, debug artifacts, commented-out code       |
216|| Traceability            | Non-obvious decisions documented with "why" comments        |
217|| Test coverage           | New code has tests, existing tests still pass               |
218|| Dependency audit        | No new high/critical vulnerabilities introduced             |
219|
220|## Context-Aware Review
221|
222|Surface-level static analysis catches formatting and basic lint issues but misses deeper problems. Effective AI code review must also assess:
223|
224|- **Architectural fit** -- does the change align with the system's design direction?
225|- **Requirement alignment** -- does the implementation match what was actually requested?
226|- **Convention consistency** -- does the code follow the team's established patterns?
227|- **Future maintainability** -- will this code be easy to modify in six months?
228|- **Integration safety** -- does the change interact correctly with existing code?
229|
230|## Quality Metrics for AI Code
231|
232|Track these metrics to measure the effectiveness of AI code review:
233|
234|| Metric                 | Target            | Why It Matters                       |
235|| ---------------------- | ----------------- | ------------------------------------ |
236|| Post-merge defect rate | <2% of AI-gen PRs | Catches issues the review missed     |
237|| Review iteration count | <3 rounds per PR  | Measures AI output quality           |
238|| Time from PR to merge  | <24 hours         | Measures review bottleneck           |
239|| Gate pass rate         | >90% on first run | Measures code generation quality     |
240|| Revert rate            | <1% of merged PRs | Measures overall process reliability |

14|
15|# Audit Rubric
16|
17|A structured rubric for executing quality audits with clear pass/warn/fail thresholds, weighted scoring, and a distinction between automated and manual audit items.
18|
19|## Pass / Warn / Fail Thresholds
20|
21|Each dimension receives a 1-10 score, then maps to a threshold:
22|
23|| Threshold | Score Range | Meaning                                         | Action Required           |
24|| --------- | ----------- | ----------------------------------------------- | ------------------------- |
25|| Pass      | 7-10        | Meets or exceeds standards                      | No action                 |
26|| Warn      | 5-6         | Below standard but functional                   | Improvement plan required |
27|| Fail      | 1-4         | Critical gaps, blocks release or further work   | Immediate remediation     |
28|| N/A       | --          | Dimension does not apply (e.g., no UI for a11y) | Redistribute weight       |
29|
30|**Hard fail conditions (override any score):**
31|
32|- Phase 0 resource completeness fails -- cap overall at 6.0
33|- Any security dimension score of 3 or below -- flag as release blocker
34|- Any critical anti-pattern found without a mitigation plan -- fail the audit
35|
36|## Dimension Rubric Summary
37|
38|Each dimension uses consistent criteria across three levels. See `dimension-rubrics.md` for full per-dimension detail.
39|
40|### Code Quality (10%)
41|
42|| Level | Criteria                                                      |
43|| ----- | ------------------------------------------------------------- |
44|| Pass  | Consistent patterns, low duplication, complexity under limits |
45|| Warn  | Some code smells, moderate duplication, complexity hotspots   |
46|| Fail  | No patterns, widespread duplication, god objects              |
47|
48|### Architecture (10%)
49|
50|| Level | Criteria                                                        |
51|| ----- | --------------------------------------------------------------- |
52|| Pass  | Clear module boundaries, low coupling, scalable design          |
53|| Warn  | Some coupling, unclear boundaries in non-critical areas         |
54|| Fail  | Circular dependencies, tight coupling, no separation of concern |
55|
56|### Documentation (10%)
57|
58|| Level | Criteria                                                   |
59|| ----- | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
60|| Pass  | All features documented, examples work, accurate to code   |
61|| Warn  | Major features documented, some gaps, some stale examples  |
62|| Fail  | Missing docs for critical paths, misleading or no examples |
63|
64|### Usability (10%)
65|
66|| Level | Criteria                                                      |
67|| ----- | ------------------------------------------------------------- |
68|| Pass  | Under 10 minutes to first success, clear error messages       |
69|| Warn  | 10-30 minutes to first success, some confusing error messages |
70|| Fail  | Over 30 minutes to first success, cryptic errors, no defaults |
71|
72|### Performance (8%)
73|
74|| Level | Criteria                                                              |
75|| ----- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- |
76|| Pass  | Within performance budget, no N+1 queries, acceptable Core Web Vitals |
77|| Warn  | Occasional slow paths, minor budget overruns, no profiling            |
78|| Fail  | Unusable latency, resource exhaustion, no optimization                |
79|
80|### Security (10%)
81|
82|| Level | Criteria                                                       |
83|| ----- | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
84|| Pass  | OWASP Top 10 addressed, inputs validated, no hardcoded secrets |
85|| Warn  | Most inputs validated, minor dependency vulnerabilities        |
86|| Fail  | Hardcoded secrets, SQL injection, missing auth on endpoints    |
87|
88|### Testing (8%)
89|
90|| Level | Criteria                                                           |
91|| ----- | ------------------------------------------------------------------ |
92|| Pass  | 80%+ coverage, unit/integration/e2e present, tests verify behavior |
93|| Warn  | 60-79% coverage, mostly unit tests, some flaky tests               |
94|| Fail  | Under 40% coverage, no integration tests, tests verify mocks       |
95|
96|### Maintainability (8%)
97|
98|| Level | Criteria                                                     |
99|| ----- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
100|| Pass  | Low tech debt, clear contribution path, semver compliance    |
101|| Warn  | Moderate debt, some outdated deps, unclear contribution path |
102|| Fail  | High debt, abandoned dependencies, no versioning strategy    |
103|
104|### Developer Experience (10%)
105|
106|| Level | Criteria                                                    |
107|| ----- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
108|| Pass  | Under 5 minutes setup, fast feedback loop, good error DX    |
109|| Warn  | 5-15 minutes setup, some friction, basic error messages     |
110|| Fail  | Over 15 minutes setup, broken tooling, no debugging support |
111|
112|### Accessibility (8%)
113|
114|| Level | Criteria                                                    |
115|| ----- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
116|| Pass  | WCAG 2.1 AA compliant, keyboard navigable, screen reader OK |
117|| Warn  | Partial WCAG compliance, keyboard works for main flows      |
118|| Fail  | No WCAG compliance, keyboard traps, inaccessible content    |
119|
120|### CI/CD (5%)
121|
122|| Level | Criteria                                             |
123|| ----- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
124|| Pass  | Automated build, test, deploy pipeline with rollback |
125|| Warn  | Automated build and test, manual deploy              |
126|| Fail  | No automation, manual build and deploy               |
127|
128|### Innovation (3%)
129|
130|| Level | Criteria                                           |
131|| ----- | -------------------------------------------------- |
132|| Pass  | Novel approach or unique value proposition         |
133|| Warn  | Conventional but competent implementation          |
134|| Fail  | Derivative with no differentiation (rarely blocks) |
135|
136|## Weighted Scoring Methodology
137|
138|### Calculating the Overall Score
139|
140|Multiply each dimension score by its weight, then sum:
141|
142|```text
143|Overall = (CodeQuality * 0.10) + (Architecture * 0.10) + (Documentation * 0.10)
144|        + (Usability * 0.10) + (Performance * 0.08) + (Security * 0.10)
145|        + (Testing * 0.08) + (Maintainability * 0.08) + (DX * 0.10)
146|        + (Accessibility * 0.08) + (CICD * 0.05) + (Innovation * 0.03)
147|```
148|
149|Round to one decimal place.
150|
151|### Handling N/A Dimensions
152|
153|When a dimension does not apply, redistribute its weight proportionally:
154|
155|```text
156|Example: CLI tool with no UI -- Accessibility (8%) is N/A
157|
158|Remaining weight = 100% - 8% = 92%
159|Adjusted weights = each remaining dimension weight / 0.92
160|
161|Code Quality: 10% / 0.92 = 10.9%
162|Security: 10% / 0.92 = 10.9%
163|...
164|```
165|
166|### Weight Adjustments by Project Type
167|
168|Customize weights based on what matters most:
169|
170|| Project Type    | Increase Weight     | Decrease Weight   |
171|| --------------- | ------------------- | ----------------- |
172|| Public API      | Security, Docs, DX  | Innovation, A11y  |
173|| Consumer Web    | A11y, Perf, UX      | CI/CD, Innovation |
174|| Internal Tool   | DX, Maintainability | A11y, Innovation  |
175|| Library/Package | Architecture, Tests | Usability, CI/CD  |
176|| CLI Tool        | DX, Usability, Docs | A11y, Perf        |
177|
178|Document any weight adjustments in the audit report with justification.
179|
180|### Score Caps
181|
182|| Condition                           | Cap |
183|| ----------------------------------- | --- |
184|| Phase 0 resource completeness fails | 6.0 |
185|| Any dimension scores 1-2            | 7.0 |
186|| Security scores 3 or below          | 5.0 |
187|| No tests exist                      | 6.0 |
188|
189|Apply the lowest applicable cap.
190|
191|## Automated vs Manual Audit Items
192|
193|### Automated Checks (Run First)
194|
195|These checks produce objective, repeatable results. Run them before manual review.
196|
197|| Check             | Tool / Command                                         | Pass Criteria             |
198|| ----------------- | ------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------- |
199|| Type safety       | `npx tsc --noEmit --strict`                            | Zero errors               |
200|| Lint              | `npx eslint . --max-warnings 0`                        | Zero errors               |
201|| Format            | `npx prettier --check .`                               | No formatting diffs       |
202|| Tests             | `npx vitest run --coverage`                            | All pass, coverage target |
203|| Security deps     | `npm audit --audit-level=high`                         | No high/critical vulns    |
204|| Bundle size       | Build output size check                                | Within budget             |
205|| Hardcoded secrets | `rg -i "(api.?key\|secret\|password\|token)\\s*[:=]"`  | Zero matches in source    |
206|| Dead code         | `rg "console\\.(log\|debug)" -g "*.ts" -g "!*.test.*"` | Zero matches              |
207|| Complexity        | SonarQube or custom threshold                          | Under configured limit    |
208|
209|### Manual Review Items
210|
211|These require human or AI judgment. Perform after automated checks pass.
212|
213|| Check                      | What to Evaluate                                           |
214|| -------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
215|| Architectural fit          | Does the code follow the system's design direction?        |
216|| Requirement alignment      | Does implementation match what was requested?              |
217|| Convention consistency     | Does code follow established team patterns?                |
218|| API design quality         | Are endpoints/interfaces intuitive, consistent, versioned? |
219|| Error handling adequacy    | Are error paths thoughtful, not just catch-and-log?        |
220|| Edge case coverage         | Are boundary conditions and failure modes handled?         |
221|| Documentation accuracy     | Does documentation match the actual implementation?        |
222|| Future maintainability     | Will this code be easy to modify in six months?            |
223|| Business logic correctness | Do calculations and rules match requirements?              |
224|| Integration safety         | Does the change interact correctly with existing code?     |
225|
226|### Audit Execution Order
227|
228|1. Run all automated checks and collect results
229|2. If any automated check fails, stop and remediate before manual review
230|3. Perform manual review items, scoring each dimension
231|4. Calculate weighted overall score
232|5. Apply score caps if any hard-fail conditions triggered
233|6. Generate the audit report
234|
235|## Audit Report Format
236|
237|Structure every audit report with these sections in order:
238|
239|```markdown
240|# Quality Audit Report: [Subject]
241|
242|**Date:** [Date]
243|**Version:** [Version]
244|**Auditor:** [Agent or person]
245|
246|## Executive Summary
247|
248|**Overall Score:** [X.X]/10 - [Pass/Warn/Fail]
249|
250|**Top 3 Strengths:** [With evidence]
251|**Top 3 Weaknesses:** [With evidence]
252|**Recommendation:** [Exceptional / Excellent / Good / Acceptable / Needs Improvement]
253|
254|## Automated Gate Results
255|
256|| Gate | Result | Details |
257|| ---- | ------ | ------- |
258|
259|## Dimension Scores
260|
261|| Dimension | Weight | Score | Level | Evidence Summary |
262|| --------- | ------ | ----- | ----- | ---------------- |
263|
264|**Weighted Overall:** [X.X]/10
265|**Caps Applied:** [None / list]
266|
267|## Findings by Priority
268|
269|### Critical (Fix Before Release)
270|
271|### High (Fix This Sprint)
272|
273|### Medium (Plan for Next Sprint)
274|
275|### Low (Backlog)
276|
277|## Recommendations
278|
279|### Quick Wins (High Impact / Low Effort)
280|
281|### Short-Term (1-3 Months)
282|
283|### Long-Term (3-12 Months)
284|
285|## Risk Matrix
286|
287|| Risk | Likelihood | Impact | Mitigation |
288|| ---- | ---------- | ------ | ---------- |
289|```
290|
291|See `audit-report-template.md` for the full template with all subsections.
292|
293|## Calibration Guidelines
294|
295|To maintain consistent scoring across audits:
296|
297|- **10/10 is rare** -- reserved for industry-leading implementations (Linux kernel code quality, Stripe documentation)
298|- **Most quality software scores 6-7** -- this is the realistic baseline
299|- **A score of 8+ means genuinely above average** -- requires strong evidence
300|- **Compare against industry leaders**, not team averages or personal standards
301|- **Every score needs evidence** -- file paths, metrics, tool output, or concrete examples
302|- **Scores without evidence are invalid** -- reject them during review

13|
14|# Anti-Patterns Guide
15|
16|A catalog of anti-patterns to identify during quality audits, organized by category. Each anti-pattern includes detection strategies and severity levels.
17|
18|## Code Anti-Patterns
19|
20|| Anti-Pattern           | Signal                                   | Severity |
21|| ---------------------- | ---------------------------------------- | -------- |
22|| God objects            | Single class/module doing everything     | High     |
23|| Spaghetti code         | No clear flow, tangled dependencies      | High     |
24|| Copy-paste programming | Duplicated blocks with minor variations  | Medium   |
25|| Magic numbers          | Unexplained literals in logic            | Medium   |
26|| Global state abuse     | Mutable shared state without controls    | High     |
27|| Deep nesting           | 4+ levels of indentation                 | Medium   |
28|| Long methods           | Functions exceeding 50 lines             | Medium   |
29|| Primitive obsession    | Using primitives instead of value types  | Low      |
30|| Feature envy           | Method uses more of another class's data | Medium   |
31|| Dead code              | Unreachable or unused code paths         | Low      |
32|| Type bypassing         | `any` and `@ts-ignore` causing drift     | High     |
33|| Debug artifacts        | `console.log` and test scaffolding left  | Medium   |
34|
35|### Detection Strategies
36|
37|```bash
38|# Find functions over 50 lines (approximate)
39|rg -c "^}" -g "*.ts" | sort -t: -k2 -rn | head -20
40|
41|# Find potential magic numbers
42|rg "\b(?:100|200|404|500|1000|3600|86400)\b" -g "*.ts" --stats
43|
44|# Find duplicated string literals
45|rg -o '"[^"]{10,}"' -g "*.ts" --no-filename | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -10
46|
47|# Find deeply nested code
48|rg "^\s{16,}" -g "*.ts" -c | sort -t: -k2 -rn
49|
50|# Find type bypassing
51|rg "(: any|as any|@ts-ignore|@ts-expect-error)" -g "*.ts" --stats
52|
53|# Find debug artifacts
54|rg "console\.(log|debug|info|warn)" -g "*.ts" -g "!*.test.*" -g "!*.spec.*"
55|```
56|
57|## Architecture Anti-Patterns
58|
59|| Anti-Pattern          | Signal                                        | Severity |
60|| --------------------- | --------------------------------------------- | -------- |
61|| Tight coupling        | Changes cascade across modules                | High     |
62|| Circular dependencies | A depends on B depends on A                   | High     |
63|| Missing abstractions  | Implementation details leak across boundaries | Medium   |
64|| Over-engineering      | Unnecessary complexity for simple problems    | Medium   |
65|| Anemic domain model   | Data structures with no behavior              | Medium   |
66|| Big ball of mud       | No discernible architecture pattern           | Critical |
67|| Leaky abstraction     | Internal details exposed through interface    | Medium   |
68|| Vendor lock-in        | Core logic depends on specific vendor APIs    | High     |
69|| Paradigm mixing       | Inconsistent patterns confuse humans and AI   | Medium   |
70|
71|### Detection Strategies
72|
73|```bash
74|# Find files importing from many different modules (high fan-out)
75|rg -c "^import" -g "*.ts" | sort -t: -k2 -rn | head -20
76|
77|# Find circular imports (approximate -- look for mutual references)
78|rg "^import.*from" -g "*.ts" --no-heading | sort > /tmp/imports.txt
79|
80|# Find barrel files that re-export everything (coupling amplifier)
81|rg "^export \* from" -g "index.ts" -g "index.tsx"
82|```
83|
84|## Security Anti-Patterns
85|
86|| Anti-Pattern             | Signal                            | Severity |
87|| ------------------------ | --------------------------------- | -------- |
88|| Hardcoded secrets        | API keys, passwords in source     | Critical |
89|| SQL injection            | Unsanitized user input in queries | Critical |
90|| XSS vulnerabilities      | Unescaped output in templates     | High     |
91|| Missing authentication   | Endpoints without auth checks     | Critical |
92|| Insecure defaults        | Debug mode in production          | High     |
93|| Excessive permissions    | Over-scoped API keys or roles     | Medium   |
94|| Missing rate limiting    | Endpoints without throttling      | Medium   |
95|| Logging sensitive data   | PII or secrets in log output      | High     |
96|| Missing input validation | No schema validation on user data | High     |
97|
98|### Detection Strategies
99|
100|```bash
101|# Find potential hardcoded secrets
102|rg -i "(api.?key|secret|password|token)\s*[:=]" -g "*.ts" -g "!*.test.*"
103|
104|# Find potential SQL injection
105|rg "query\(.*\$\{" -g "*.ts"
106|rg "execute\(.*\+" -g "*.ts"
107|
108|# Find missing auth checks in API routes
109|rg "export (async )?function (GET|POST|PUT|DELETE)" -g "*/api/**/*.ts" -l
110|
111|# Find potential XSS in React (dangerouslySetInnerHTML)
112|rg "dangerouslySetInnerHTML" -g "*.tsx"
113|
114|# Check for sensitive data in logs
115|rg "console\.\w+\(.*(?:password|secret|token|key)" -g "*.ts" -i
116|```
117|
118|## Testing Anti-Patterns
119|
120|| Anti-Pattern              | Signal                                          | Severity |
121|| ------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- | -------- |
122|| No tests                  | Zero coverage                                   | Critical |
123|| Flaky tests               | Non-deterministic pass/fail                     | High     |
124|| Test duplication          | Same scenario tested multiple ways              | Medium   |
125|| Testing implementation    | Tests break on refactor without behavior change | High     |
126|| Missing edge cases        | Only happy path tested                          | Medium   |
127|| Slow tests                | Test suite takes >10 minutes                    | Medium   |
128|| Test pollution            | Tests depend on execution order                 | High     |
129|| Over-mocking              | Tests verify mocks, not behavior                | Medium   |
130|| Snapshot abuse            | Snapshots used as primary assertion strategy    | Medium   |
131|| Missing integration tests | Only unit tests, no integration coverage        | High     |
132|
133|### Detection Strategies
134|
135|```bash
136|# Check test coverage
137|npx vitest --coverage --reporter=json
138|
139|# Find tests without assertions
140|rg "it\(|test\(" -A 20 -g "*.test.*" | rg -v "expect\(|assert"
141|
142|# Find snapshot-heavy test files
143|rg "toMatchSnapshot|toMatchInlineSnapshot" -c -g "*.test.*" | sort -t: -k2 -rn
144|
145|# Find tests with timeouts (flaky test signal)
146|rg "setTimeout|waitFor|sleep" -g "*.test.*" -c | sort -t: -k2 -rn
147|```
148|
149|## Process Anti-Patterns
150|
151|| Anti-Pattern           | Why It Fails                          | Correct Alternative         |
152|| ---------------------- | ------------------------------------- | --------------------------- |
153|| "LGTM" mentality       | Superficial review hides deep bugs    | Deep semantic audit         |
154|| Bypassing types        | `any` and `@ts-ignore` cause drift    | Total type integrity        |
155|| Mixing paradigms       | Confuses AI context and humans        | Strict pattern consistency  |
156|| Silent delivery        | User does not know what was validated | Verification reporting      |
157|| Debt for speed         | "We'll fix it later" = never          | Zero-debt policy            |
158|| No code ownership      | Nobody responsible for quality        | Clear ownership model       |
159|| Review without context | Reviewer lacks domain knowledge       | Domain-expert review        |
160|| AI trust without check | AI-generated code accepted blindly    | Verification gap protocol   |
161|| Score inflation        | Giving high scores without evidence   | Evidence-based scoring only |
162|
163|## Pre-Commit Audit Checklist
164|
165|Before declaring any task finished, verify:
166|
167|1. **Contract integrity** -- code matches defined interfaces (Zod schemas, TypeScript types)
168|2. **Architectural alignment** -- idiomatic patterns for the stack in use
169|3. **Security sanitization** -- all inputs validated, no secrets in logs or code
170|4. **Performance hygiene** -- no N+1 queries, images optimized, bundle size checked
171|5. **Cleanliness audit** -- no `console.log`, debug artifacts, or commented-out code
172|6. **Traceability** -- the "why" is documented for non-obvious decisions (comments or ADRs)
173|
174|## Risk-Based PR Categorization
175|
176|Categorize changes by risk level to allocate review effort appropriately:
177|
178|| Risk Level | Examples                                     | Review Strategy               |
179|| ---------- | -------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------- |
180|| Critical   | Auth logic, payment flows, schema migrations | Human expert review           |
181|| High       | API contracts, cross-service changes         | Senior engineer review        |
182|| Medium     | Feature code, UI components                  | Standard code review          |
183|| Low        | Config changes, dependency bumps, typo fixes | Automated review + spot check |
184|
185|Route high-risk changes to domain experts. Auto-approve low-risk, well-scoped changes that pass automated gates. Flag unrelated changes bundled in the same PR for separation.

5|
6|# Verification Before Completion
7|
8|## Overview
9|
10|**Core principle:** Evidence before claims, always.
11|
12|**Violating the letter of this rule is violating the spirit of this rule.**
13|
14|## The Iron Law
15|
16|```
17|NO COMPLETION CLAIMS WITHOUT FRESH VERIFICATION EVIDENCE
18|```
19|
20|If you haven't run the verification command in this message, you cannot claim it passes.
21|
22|## The Gate Function
23|
24|```
25|BEFORE claiming any status or expressing satisfaction:
26|
27|1. IDENTIFY: What command proves this claim?
28|2. RUN: Execute the FULL command (fresh, complete)
29|3. READ: Full output, check exit code, count failures
30|4. VERIFY: Does output confirm the claim?
31|   - If NO: State actual status with evidence
32|   - If YES: State claim WITH evidence
33|5. ONLY THEN: Make the claim
34|
35|Skip any step = lying, not verifying
36|```
37|
38|## Common Failures
39|
40|| Claim | Requires | Not Sufficient |
41||-------|----------|----------------|
42|| Tests pass | Test command output: 0 failures | Previous run, "should pass" |
43|| Linter clean | Linter output: 0 errors | Partial check, extrapolation |
44|| Build succeeds | Build command: exit 0 | Linter passing, logs look good |
45|| Bug fixed | Test original symptom: passes | Code changed, assumed fixed |
46|| Regression test works | Red-green cycle verified | Test passes once |
47|| Agent completed | VCS diff shows changes | Agent reports "success" |
48|| Requirements met | Line-by-line checklist | Tests passing |
49|
50|## Red Flags - STOP
51|
52|- Using "should", "probably", "seems to"
53|- Expressing satisfaction before verification ("Great!", "Perfect!", "Done!", etc.)
54|- About to commit/push/PR without verification
55|- Trusting agent success reports
56|- Relying on partial verification
57|- Thinking "just this once"
58|- Tired and wanting work over
59|- **ANY wording implying success without having run verification**
60|
61|## Rationalization Prevention
62|
63|| Excuse | Reality |
64||--------|---------|
65|| "Should work now" | RUN the verification |
66|| "I'm confident" | Confidence ≠ evidence |
67|| "Just this once" | No exceptions |
68|| "Linter passed" | Linter ≠ compiler |
69|| "Agent said success" | Verify independently |
70|| "I'm tired" | Exhaustion ≠ excuse |
71|| "Partial check is enough" | Partial proves nothing |
72|| "Different words so rule doesn't apply" | Spirit over letter |
73|
74|## Key Patterns
75|
76|**Tests:**
77|```
78|✅ [Run test command] [See: 34/34 pass] "All tests pass"
79|❌ "Should pass now" / "Looks correct"
80|```
81|
82|**Regression tests (TDD Red-Green):**
83|```
84|✅ Write → Run (pass) → Revert fix → Run (MUST FAIL) → Restore → Run (pass)
85|❌ "I've written a regression test" (without red-green verification)
86|```
87|
88|**Build:**
89|```
90|✅ [Run build] [See: exit 0] "Build passes"
91|❌ "Linter passed" (linter doesn't check compilation)
92|```
93|
94|**Requirements:**
95|```
96|✅ Re-read plan → Create checklist → Verify each → Report gaps or completion
97|❌ "Tests pass, phase complete"
98|```
99|
100|**Agent delegation:**
101|```
102|✅ Agent reports success → Check VCS diff → Verify changes → Report actual state
103|❌ Trust agent report
104|```
105|
106|## When To Apply
107|
108|**ALWAYS before:**
109|- ANY variation of success/completion claims
110|- ANY expression of satisfaction
111|- ANY positive statement about work state
112|- Committing, PR creation, task completion
113|- Moving to next task
114|- Delegating to agents
115|
116|**Rule applies to:**
117|- Exact phrases
118|- Paraphrases and synonyms
119|- Implications of success
120|- ANY communication suggesting completion/correctness

6|
7|# Agent Self-Evaluation
8|
9|After completing a complex task, the agent pauses to rate its own output against a structured 5-axis rubric. This is NOT a pass/fail gate — it's a deliberate reflection step that catches omissions, flags overconfidence, and surface areas for improvement before the user has to.
10|
11|## When to Activate
12|
13|- After writing code that spans 3+ files or 50+ lines
14|- After completing a multi-step workflow (implement → test → review)
15|- After a debugging session that involved 3+ attempts
16|- After producing a design document, architecture decision, or written analysis
17|- When the user asks "how good was that?" or "rate yourself"
18|- At the end of any session Stop hook (if configured — see `references/hook-integration.md`)
19|
20|## Core Concepts
21|
22|### The 5 Evaluation Axes
23|
24|| Axis | Question | What it catches |
25||---|---|---|
26|| **Accuracy** | Are the facts, claims, and outputs correct? | Hallucinations, wrong API names, incorrect syntax, false statements |
27|| **Completeness** | Did it cover everything the user asked for? | Missed edge cases, unhandled error paths, forgotten requirements, skipped subtasks |
28|| **Clarity** | Is the explanation understandable and well-structured? | Confusing explanations, jargon without definition, missing context, rambling |
29|| **Actionability** | Can the user act on the output immediately? | Vague suggestions, missing steps, "you should X" without showing how, no verification path |
30|| **Conciseness** | Did it use the minimum words/tokens needed? | Redundancy, over-explanation, repeating the user's question verbatim, filler content |
31|
32|### Scoring Scale
33|
34|```
35|5 — Exceptional: no reasonable improvement possible
36|4 — Good: minor nits only, no substantive gaps
37|3 — Adequate: meets the request but has a notable weakness on at least one axis
38|2 — Weak: has a clear gap that affects usability or correctness
39|1 — Poor: fundamentally misses the request or contains significant errors
40|```
41|
42|### The Evidence Rule
43|
44|Every score below 5 MUST cite specific evidence. A score of 3 cannot just say "could be better" — it must say exactly what is missing or wrong. The mantra: **"Show the gap, don't just name it."**
45|
46|## Workflow
47|
48|### Step 1: Collect the Raw Material
49|
50|Gather what you'll evaluate:
51|
52|```
53|- The original user request (read back from conversation)
54|- Your final response/output (the deliverable)
55|- Any tool outputs that verify correctness (test results, exit codes, lint output)
56|- Any user feedback received during the task (corrections, "try again", "that's not right")
57|```
58|
59|### Step 2: Score Each Axis Independently
60|
61|Work through the 5 axes one at a time. For each:
62|
63|1. Read the axis question
64|2. Find evidence (or lack of evidence) in the output
65|3. Assign a score 1-5
66|4. If score < 5, write a one-sentence improvement note citing the gap
67|
68|Do NOT average the scores in your head first and then work backwards. Score each axis fresh.
69|
70|### Step 3: Produce the Evaluation Report
71|
72|Use the template from `templates/evaluation-report.md`. The report must include:
73|
74|```
75|- One-line summary
76|- 5-axis scorecard (score + evidence per axis)
77|- Overall score (simple average, rounded to 1 decimal)
78|- 1-3 specific improvements ranked by impact
79|- Self-check: "Would the user agree with this assessment?"
80|```
81|
82|### Step 4: Apply the Improvement
83|
84|If any axis scored 3 or below:
85|
86|1. State what you would do differently
87|2. If the gap is fixable in < 30 seconds (missing link, unclear phrasing), fix it now
88|3. If the gap requires rework, flag it explicitly: "This axis scored [reason] because [evidence]. Re-running with [specific fix] would likely raise it to [score]."
89|
90|## Code Examples
91|
92|### Example: Good Evaluation (Score 4+)
93|
94|```
95|Task: Add retry logic to HTTP client
96|
97|Scorecard:
98|  Accuracy:    5 — All API calls correct. Verified: retries use
99|                  exponential backoff. No hallucinated methods.
100|  Completeness: 4 — Covered happy path + 3 error cases. Missing:
101|                  timeout handling for hung connections.
102|  Clarity:      5 — Code comments explain backoff formula.
103|                  PR description links to incident that motivated this.
104|  Actionability:5 — Single merge. No follow-up tasks. Tests pass.
105|  Conciseness:  4 — 47 lines total. The retry loop could be extracted
106|                  into a helper to drop ~8 lines.
107|
108|Overall: 4.6 — One gap (timeout handling). Fix before merging.
109|```
110|
111|### Example: Weak Evaluation (Score 2-3)
112|
113|```
114|Task: Add retry logic to HTTP client
115|
116|Scorecard:
117|  Accuracy:    2 — Used urllib3 which doesn't match our
118|                  httpx-based codebase. Wrong library.
119|  Completeness: 3 — Works for GET. POST/PUT not handled (user
120|                  said "all HTTP requests").
121|  Clarity:      4 — Code is readable. Good variable names.
122|  Actionability:2 — "Add tests" mentioned but no test file created.
123|                  User has to write tests before merging.
124|  Conciseness:  3 — 120 lines. The retry config is duplicated in
125|                  3 places instead of one shared RetryConfig object.
126|
127|Overall: 2.8 — Wrong library used. Needs httpx rewrite.
128|  Fix accuracy first (switch to httpx), then extend to all
129|  HTTP methods, then consolidate config.
130|```
131|
132|## Anti-Patterns
133|
134|### "Everything is a 5"
135|
136|```
137|FAIL: Accuracy:    5 — All good.
138|   Completeness: 5 — Everything covered.
139|   Clarity:      5 — Clear.
140|```
141|
142|No evidence cited. This is self-congratulation, not evaluation. A real 5 requires proving there's nothing to improve.
143|
144|### Over-penalizing for scope creep
145|
146|```
147|FAIL: Completeness: 2 — Didn't handle WebSocket connections or
148|   gRPC streaming (user didn't ask for these)
149|```
150|
151|Only evaluate against what the user actually requested, not what you could have additionally built.
152|
153|### Using the evaluation to re-litigate
154|
155|```
156|FAIL: "As I said earlier, this approach is wrong. Score: 1"
157|```
158|
159|The evaluation is about the delivered output, not about re-arguing design decisions that were already made. If the approach was wrong, that should have been caught before delivery.
160|
161|### Mixing personal preference with objective gaps
162|
163|```
164|FAIL: "Score: 3. I don't like Python decorators."
165|```
166|
167|"Don't like" is not evidence. Cite a concrete readability, testability, or correctness concern, or leave the score at 4+.
168|
169|## Best Practices
170|
171|- **Evaluate the output, not the process.** The user cares about what you delivered, not how many iterations you took.
172|- **One improvement per weak axis.** Don't list 5 things for one axis — pick the highest-impact gap.
173|- **Tie improvements to user impact.** "Missing error handling means the user's API call will crash silently" beats "add error handling."
174|- **Be specific about what 'fixed' looks like.** "Re-run with httpx transport configured for retries" beats "fix the library issue."
175|- **Use tool outputs as evidence.** If tests passed, cite them. If lint is clean, cite it. Don't guess — grep for the proof.
176|- **If you can't find any gaps, try harder.** A perfect score across all 5 axes is rare. Ask: "If I were the user, what would annoy me about this output?"
177|
178|## Related Skills
179|
180|- `agent-eval` — Head-to-head comparison of different coding agents on benchmark tasks
181|- `verification-loop` — Systematic verification of outputs against expected results
182|- `security-review` — Security-focused code review checklist

10|
11|# Security
12|
13|Security is built-in, not bolted-on. Every feature, endpoint, and data flow must consider security implications.
14|
15|## OWASP Top 10 (2025)
16|
17|| #   | Vulnerability                      | Prevention                                      |
18|| --- | ---------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- |
19|| 1   | Broken Access Control              | Verify permissions server-side, default deny    |
20|| 2   | Security Misconfiguration          | Secure defaults, remove unused features         |
21|| 3   | Software Supply Chain Failures     | SBOM, dependency scanning, signed builds        |
22|| 4   | Cryptographic Failures             | Use TLS, hash passwords (argon2id), encrypt PII |
23|| 5   | Injection                          | Parameterized queries, input validation         |
24|| 6   | Insecure Design                    | Threat modeling, security requirements          |
25|| 7   | Authentication Failures            | Strong passwords, MFA, secure session mgmt      |
26|| 8   | Software or Data Integrity         | Verify dependencies, sign releases              |
27|| 9   | Logging and Alerting Failures      | Log security events, set up alerts              |
28|| 10  | Mishandling Exceptional Conditions | Fail securely, generic errors to clients        |
29|
30|## Security Principles
31|
32|| Principle          | Rule                                                      |
33|| ------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------- |
34|| Defense in Depth   | Multiple layers: firewall, auth, authz, encryption, audit |
35|| Least Privilege    | Minimum permissions needed, nothing more                  |
36|| Zero Trust         | Never trust, always verify. Assume breach.                |
37|| Secure by Default  | HTTPS, strict passwords, secure cookies out of the box    |
38|| Fail Securely      | Access denied on error, no internal details to users      |
39|| Validate on Server | Client validation is UX, server validation is security    |
40|
41|## Pre-Deployment Checklist
42|
43|| Area          | Requirements                                                        |
44|| ------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
45|| Passwords     | Hashed with argon2id (preferred) or bcrypt (12+ rounds)             |
46|| Tokens        | JWT with EdDSA/ES256, 15min access / 7d refresh, httpOnly cookies   |
47|| Sessions      | HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Strict cookies                           |
48|| Rate Limiting | Auth endpoints: 5 attempts/15min                                    |
49|| Authorization | All routes check auth server-side, default deny                     |
50|| Input         | Validated with schema (Zod), parameterized SQL                      |
51|| Uploads       | Whitelist types, enforce size limits                                |
52|| Secrets       | No secrets in code or VCS                                           |
53|| Headers       | CSP (with nonces), HSTS, Permissions-Policy, X-Content-Type-Options |
54|| CORS          | Configured restrictively                                            |
55|| Encryption    | PII encrypted at rest (AES-256) and in transit (TLS 1.3)            |
56|| Logging       | Audit logging for security events                                   |
57|| Dependencies  | SBOM generated, `npm audit` clean, Dependabot enabled               |
58|
59|## Threat Modeling (STRIDE)
60|
61|| Threat                 | Category        | Key Mitigations                                        |
62|| ---------------------- | --------------- | ------------------------------------------------------ |
63|| Spoofing               | Authentication  | MFA, strong passwords, JWT with short expiry           |
64|| Tampering              | Integrity       | Input validation, HTTPS/TLS, signed tokens             |
65|| Repudiation            | Accountability  | Audit logging, digital signatures                      |
66|| Info Disclosure        | Confidentiality | Encryption, least privilege, secret management         |
67|| Denial of Service      | Availability    | Rate limiting, input validation, CDN/DDoS protection   |
68|| Elevation of Privilege | Authorization   | Authz checks on every request, ABAC, permission audits |
69|
70|## Risk Levels
71|
72|| Level    | Action                    |
73|| -------- | ------------------------- |
74|| Critical | Immediate action required |
75|| High     | Address before launch     |
76|| Medium   | Address post-launch       |
77|| Low      | Monitor, may accept risk  |
78|
79|## Compliance Overview
80|
81|| Framework | Scope              | Key Requirements                                                   |
82|| --------- | ------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------ |
83|| GDPR      | EU data subjects   | Consent, data subject rights, breach notification (72h), DPIA      |
84|| HIPAA     | US healthcare data | PHI encryption, RBAC, audit logs, BAA with providers               |
85|| SOC 2     | SaaS customer data | Security policies, MFA, encryption, incident response              |
86|| PCI-DSS   | Credit card data   | Use payment processor (Stripe), tokenization, network segmentation |
87|
88|## Anti-Patterns
89|
90|| Anti-Pattern                                  | Fix                                              |
91|| --------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------ |
92|| Security as afterthought                      | Integrate from design phase                      |
93|| Client-side authorization                     | Always verify permissions server-side            |
94|| Trusting client data (e.g., userId from body) | Get user ID from authenticated session           |
95|| Rolling your own crypto                       | Use proven libraries (argon2, bcrypt, libsodium) |
96|| Compliance = security                         | Compliance is the minimum; security is ongoing   |
97|| Verbose error responses                       | Generic messages to clients, details server-side |
98|
99|## Common Mistakes
100|
101|| Mistake                                                       | Correct Pattern                                                     |
102|| ------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
103|| Performing authorization checks only on the client side       | Always verify permissions server-side; client checks are UX only    |
104|| Trusting user-supplied IDs from request body (e.g., userId)   | Derive user identity from the authenticated session or token        |
105|| Rolling custom cryptography instead of using proven libraries | Use argon2id, bcrypt, or libsodium for all cryptographic operations |
106|| Treating compliance certification as equivalent to security   | Compliance is the minimum bar; security requires ongoing review     |
107|| Returning verbose error messages with stack traces to clients | Show generic messages to clients; log details server-side only      |
108|
109|## Delegation

111|- **Scan codebase for OWASP Top 10 vulnerabilities and insecure patterns**: Use `Explore` agent to search for SQL injection, XSS, and hardcoded secrets
112|- **Implement authentication, authorization, and security headers end-to-end**: Use `Task` agent to configure JWT, RBAC, CSP, HSTS, and rate limiting
113|- **Design a threat model and security architecture for new features**: Use `Plan` agent to apply STRIDE methodology and map trust boundaries

115|> For database-layer security (RLS policies, Postgres/Supabase hardening, audit trails), use the `database-security` skill. For AI/LLM security (prompt injection defense, agentic zero-trust, MCP tool hardening), use the `secure-ai` skill.

122|- [Input Validation](references/input-validation.md) — SQL injection, XSS, command injection, path traversal, Zod validation, file upload security
123|- [Data Protection](references/data-protection.md) — Password hashing (argon2id/bcrypt), AES-256-GCM encryption, secrets management
124|- [Secure Configuration](references/secure-config.md) — Security headers, CORS, Express hardening, rate limiting

15|# Rust
16|
17|## Overview
18|
19|Rust is a systems programming language focused on safety, concurrency, and performance. The ownership system guarantees memory safety without garbage collection, and the type system enforces thread safety at compile time.
20|
21|**When to use:** Systems programming, web services (axum), CLI tools (clap), terminal UIs (ratatui), WebAssembly, performance-critical applications, anything requiring memory safety without runtime overhead.
22|
23|**When NOT to use:** Rapid prototyping where compile times matter more than safety, simple scripting tasks, projects where the team has no Rust experience and deadlines are tight.
24|
25|## Quick Reference
26|
27|| Pattern             | API / Tool                          | Key Points                           |
28|| ------------------- | ----------------------------------- | ------------------------------------ |
29|| Ownership transfer  | `let b = a;`                        | `a` is moved, no longer usable       |
30|| Borrowing           | `&T` / `&mut T`                     | One mutable OR many immutable refs   |
31|| Lifetime annotation | `fn f<'a>(x: &'a str) -> &'a str`   | Ties output lifetime to input        |
32|| Error propagation   | `?` operator                        | Converts and propagates errors       |
33|| Custom errors       | `thiserror::Error` derive           | Structured error types with Display  |
34|| Ad-hoc errors       | `anyhow::Result<T>`                 | Context chaining for applications    |
35|| Async runtime       | `#[tokio::main]`                    | Entry point for async programs       |
36|| Spawn task          | `tokio::spawn(async { })`           | Concurrent async task execution      |
37|| HTTP router         | `axum::Router::new().route(...)`    | Composable routing with extractors   |
38|| Extractors          | `Json<T>`, `Path<T>`, `State<T>`    | Type-safe request parsing            |
39|| Serialization       | `#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]` | serde with format-agnostic derives   |
40|| CLI parsing         | `#[derive(Parser)]`                 | clap derive API for arg parsing      |
41|| TUI rendering       | `terminal.draw(\|f\| { })`          | Immediate-mode ratatui rendering     |
42|| Benchmarking        | `criterion::Criterion`              | Statistical benchmarking framework   |
43|| Dep auditing        | `cargo deny check`                  | License, vulnerability, source audit |
44|| Binary release      | `cargo dist init`                   | Cross-platform binary distribution   |
45|| Changelog           | `release-plz update`                | Auto semver bump and changelog       |
46|
47|## Common Mistakes
48|
49|| Mistake                                 | Correct Pattern                               |
50|| --------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- |
51|| Returning reference to local variable   | Return owned type or use lifetime parameter   |
52|| Using `unwrap()` in library code        | Return `Result` and let caller decide         |
53|| `clone()` to satisfy borrow checker     | Restructure code to avoid the borrow conflict |
54|| Blocking in async context               | Use `tokio::task::spawn_blocking`             |
55|| Shared mutable state without sync       | Use `Arc<Mutex<T>>` or channels               |
56|| `String` where `&str` suffices          | Accept `&str` in function parameters          |
57|| Ignoring `must_use` warnings            | Handle or explicitly discard with `let _ =`   |
58|| Large enum variants                     | Box the large variant to reduce overall size  |
59|| `async fn` in traits without bounds     | Add `Send` bound or use `async-trait` crate   |
60|| Missing `#[tokio::test]` on async tests | Use `#[tokio::test]` instead of `#[test]`     |
61|
